To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
estrogen stimulates hepatic vitellogenin synthesis in reptiles and that progesterone inhibits this process.
The evolution of mammalian sex differences in hepatic lipid metabolism and its regulation by steroid hormones can be better understood from a phylogenetic perspective.

1) the phylogenetic trend toward viviparity has involved the evolution of complex hormonal control of hepatic protein-lipoprotein synthesis; 2) this control is mediated by a combination of ovarian steroids and pituitary hormones; and 3) this complex hormonal control has been conserved in mammals, and thus may be relevant to cardiovascular disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the endocrine control of hepatic protein synthesis and its relevance to the evolution of mammalian reproductive physiology and pathology.
the regulation of sex-differentiated liver function in reptiles and mammals, with particular emphasis on hepatic yolk protein synthesis and lipoprotein synthesis, respectively.
the evolution of the endocrine regulation of yolk protein and lipoprotein synthesis in the vertebrates, with particular reference to the reptiles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
reptilian hepatic protein-lipoprotein synthesis is a model for mammal liver function and that the endocrine regulation of these functions is complex and may be better studied in the reptilian model.
the control of yolt protein synthesis in reptiles is complex and involves the pituitary and gonads.
the phylogeny of the control of vitellogenin synthesis is complex and not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the reptilian model is an ideal system for studying sex-differentiated protein synthesis in the liver and the hormonal regulation of these functions, which are phylogenetically related to mammalian lipoprotein metabolism and cardiovascular disease.

in reptiles the regulation of yolk protein (vitelline) synthesis is a complex function involving both pituitaries and ovarian steroids and that these functions have been conserved in mammals and are of particular relevance to the understanding of sex-biased cardiovascular disease in humans.
in both mammals and reptiles there is a complex hormonal control of sex-differentiated liver functions, which is phylogenetically derived.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the context of the phylogenetic history of vertebrates, estrogen and progesterone have a complex and dynamic relationship in the control of hepatic protein synthesis in female vertebrates.

the evolution of viviparous reproductive physiology in mammals involved a complex series of hormonal interactions which are still relevant today and which may have a bearing on the development of cardiovascular disease.
the evolution of the mammalian liver has been complex and has involved the suppression of vitellogenin synthesis as a consequence of the evolution of the placenta.
